correctness.rationale: From the product formula, odd n>=5 has L_2(n)>=3 and L_2(n)=3 exactly at n=5,9,15. Hence D_2(n)>=4, equality at exactly those three n. Geometric iteration sums give all p=2,3,5 formulas. For p>=7, a=1 gives D_2(p)-p=D_2(p-2)-2>=2 with equality at p=7,11,17; for a>=2 the first two iterates exceed p^a by at least (p-6)p^(a-2), and the third adds at least 3. Independent exact-iterates test across 1776 prime powers supports but does not replace the proof.

originality.rationale: Theorem 3.5 of the 2015 defining paper establishes infinite selected abundant prime-power rays, not universal p>=7 abundance and sharp gap. Its deficiency results at p=3,5 are explicitly attributed to prior work. The 2010 exceptional-unit paper treats iteration lengths rather than sums. published-finding corpus and web searches located no statement or table that implies the all-prime classification. Shortness of proof leaves a residual risk of historical rediscovery.
residual_risks: Potential older unpublished or poorly indexed classification, especially as proof uses elementary local factors.

value.rationale: The 2015 source explicitly raises the question of further D_m-perfect integers. This theorem gives a complete infinite classification for the natural prime-power domain of m=2, proves no prime-power solution, identifies a sharp phase transition at p=7 that holds uniformly in exponent, and determines the exact smallest abundant surplus and all three minimizers. It does not purport to settle multi-prime-support perfectness.
